edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: New signals from Ukraine peace efforts, a looming debate over UK interest rates and fresh Danish reporting on public services, technology and history.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises developments and reporting with clear public consequence. Returning stories are included only where the gather provides a meaningful update; claims and proposals remain attributed and unresolved questions are noted.

content.headline: Zelensky says US floated Donbas-for-Nato deal in peace talks
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky: US floated Donbas-for-Nato deal
content.standfirst: Volodymyr Zelensky says US envoys asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the Donbas in exchange for Nato membership. He says Kyiv will not give up territory and would put any concrete proposal with guarantees to a referendum.

image.caption: Zelensky with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

sources.originalTitle: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Zelenskyy accuses SpaceX of lying about Starshield – and says US floated Donbas-for-Nato deal
Ekspert: Amerikansk forslag om ukrainsk Nato-medlemskab er 'helt urealistisk'

segments.body: Zelensky says US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the possibility of Ukraine withdrawing from the Donbas in return for Nato membership or security guarantees. He says the details were vague and that no proposal appeared to include US peacekeeping troops. Zelensky has ruled out ceding more Ukrainian territory.

segments.title: A deal with major obstacles
segments.body: Zelensky says he would put a proposal to a referendum if it included security guarantees, no limits on Ukraine’s military and funds for reconstruction. Russia has demanded territorial concessions and neutrality, while Kyiv says those terms would leave it exposed to another invasion. Zelensky also says Ukraine’s Starshield connections have been restricted along the front line; he disputes SpaceX’s account that the problem is technical.

perspectives.body: DIIS researcher Flemming Splidsboel calls the proposed exchange “completely unrealistic” from Russia’s perspective, arguing Moscow would likely demand further limits on Ukraine and its security arrangements.

content.headline: White House says Trump, Putin and Xi plan meeting in China
content.shortHeadline: White House says Trump, Putin and Xi plan China meeting
content.standfirst: The White House says the three leaders plan to meet during next week’s Apec summit, with nuclear arms reduction on the agenda. Russia has confirmed the meeting, while China has not yet commented.

image.caption: The White House says Trump, Putin and Xi plan to meet next week.

sources.originalTitle: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says

segments.body: White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales says Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping plan a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. She says Trump wants to discuss reducing nuclear weapons. Russia has confirmed the meeting; China has yet to respond.

segments.title: Arms control in focus
segments.body: The US-Russia treaty limiting their nuclear arsenals expired in February, leaving the two countries without major arms-control guardrails. A senior US official cited by news agencies said no agreement was expected to follow the planned talks.

content.headline: Hungary finds nearly $20m in probe of former Orbán-era minister
content.shortHeadline: Hungary finds nearly $20m in former minister probe
content.standfirst: Authorities say cash worth $19.5m was found in safes, buildings and woodland during an investigation into alleged bribery involving a state transport company. Former minister Miklós Seszták denies wrongdoing.

image.caption: Cash seized in the investigation has been deposited in Hungary’s national treasury.

source.credit: The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH)

sources.originalTitle: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister

segments.body: Hungarian investigators say they found cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) in safes, farm and residential buildings, warehouses and woodland. The search is part of a probe into former national development minister Miklós Seszták, who is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company. He denies wrongdoing.

segments.title: A test of the new government’s pledge
segments.body: The investigation is part of the new government’s anti-corruption drive, launched after Péter Magyar defeated Viktor Orbán in April. Magyar called the discovery the end of the “mafia”. Orbán has rejected allegations of corruption and described other investigations into his former government as political revenge.

content.headline: Man found dead on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
content.shortHeadline: Man found dead after attempted Channel crossing
content.standfirst: French authorities say a man in his twenties was found on Sainte-Cécile beach after a chaotic attempt to board an overloaded small boat. The circumstances of his death remain under investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing

segments.body: The French coastguard says a man in his twenties was found dead on Sainte-Cécile beach near Le Touquet on Saturday morning. Authorities had stopped a makeshift boat from leaving overnight. They described the boarding as chaotic and said a search of the water found no one before the man’s body was discovered.

An investigation is to establish what happened. In the latest UK figures cited in the report, 903 people arrived by small boat in the week ending 8 November, while 624 were prevented from making the crossing.

content.headline: Bank of England economist signals further rate rises to curb inflation
content.shortHeadline: Bank economist signals more rate rises
content.standfirst: Chief economist Huw Pill says the Bank may need to raise rates again as inflation pressures persist. His warning comes as millions of homeowners face refinancing, while businesses and households may be hit by higher borrowing costs.

sources.originalTitle: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says

segments.body: Huw Pill, the Bank of England’s chief economist, says further interest-rate rises may be needed after the Bank lifted its rate to 4% this month. He says inflation could rise to 5% next spring and that he worries about higher costs feeding into wages and prices. Financial markets expect rates to approach 5% in 2027.

segments.title: The costs and risks
segments.body: The report says an estimated 2.3 million homeowners will have to refinance next year. Pill’s outlook is not universally shared: concerns include the effect of higher borrowing costs on manufacturing, construction and household spending, as energy and council-tax bills are also expected to rise.

content.headline: Burnham says UK has lost more than it gained since Brexit
content.shortHeadline: Burnham says UK lost out after Brexit
content.standfirst: Ahead of next week’s UK-EU summit, Andy Burnham says Britain has lost more than it gained from leaving the bloc. Talks on food, trade and other areas are progressing, but key terms remain unresolved.

image.caption: Andy Burnham addresses the Welsh Labour conference in Llandudno.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
Everything that’s on the line for UK’s Brexit reset deal
UK on cusp of historic Brexit deal as hopes grow last obstacle can be overcome

segments.body: Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference, Andy Burnham said the UK had “lost more than we’ve gained” over the past decade and accused the Conservatives of making Brexit harsher than voters expected. He says a deal on food and farming is a priority at next week’s summit and could help lower costs and support Welsh businesses.

segments.title: Terms still under discussion
segments.body: Negotiations include food trade, emissions and a youth mobility scheme, as well as British access to the EU’s proposed Made in Europe industrial programme. UK and EU sources describe progress, but tuition fees for EU students and the UK’s approach to EU rules remain sticking points. The sides have not yet reached a final deal.

content.headline: UK and EU plan to share medicine-supply information amid shortages
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU plan to share medicine-supply data
content.standfirst: A proposed health-security agreement would let Britain and the EU share information about medicine shortages and where supplies are available. It is expected to be part of next week’s summit package, but has not yet been finalised.

image.caption: Augmentin tablets on a pharmaceutical production line in France.

sources.originalTitle: Pharmacies to have better access to antibiotics and ADHD drugs in new Brexit deal

segments.body: A draft UK-EU statement points to a health-security agreement on sharing information about medicine supplies and shortages. The deal is expected to be discussed at the 20 November summit. A health think-tank expert calls earlier information useful for helping authorities locate available stocks and respond before shortages affect patients.

segments.title: Shortages affecting patients
segments.body: The report says shortages have affected antibiotics and medicines for conditions including ADHD and epilepsy. It also cites shortfalls of Creon, used by some people with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic problems, and the stomach treatment Lanzoprazole. The proposed information-sharing agreement would not itself guarantee supplies or resolve the wider causes of shortages.

content.headline: Labour MPs warn youth benefit reforms could leave disabled claimants worse off
content.shortHeadline: Labour MPs challenge planned youth benefit changes
content.standfirst: Alan Milburn’s forthcoming review is expected to propose moving some under-25s from existing disability-related benefits to a new youth allowance. Labour MPs are divided, with critics warning some could lose support.

image.caption: Alan Milburn is leading a review of support for young people not in work, education or training.

sources.originalTitle: ‘No one wants to see cuts’: Labour MPs sound alarm over youth benefits reforms

segments.body: Alan Milburn’s review of young people not in work, education or training is due on Tuesday. In reported proposals, under-25s would no longer receive the health element of Universal Credit or Personal Independence Payment, but could move to a standard-rate youth allowance with additional disability support in some cases. The government says it will respond to the recommendations in full.

segments.title: Divided over the impact
segments.body: Several Labour MPs warn that existing claimants could initially receive less support and say benefit cuts should not replace help to overcome barriers to work. Others say they are willing to consider the review’s proposals, particularly its focus on employment support. The full recommendations have not yet been published.

content.headline: Care visa changes raise fears of shortages in areas reliant on overseas staff
content.shortHeadline: Care visa changes fuel concern over staffing gaps
content.standfirst: Analysis finds overseas workers make up a large share of direct-care staff in some English areas. Care leaders warn that visa and settlement changes could worsen recruitment problems, though the precise local impact is uncertain.

image.caption: Recruitment to the UK care sector has fallen by tens of thousands.

sources.originalTitle: The areas where vulnerable people could lose care due to Labour’s visa clampdown

segments.body: International recruitment into care has fallen since the government stopped issuing new health and care worker visas in July 2025. The report’s analysis finds that non-British workers made up 84% of direct-care staff in Barking and Dagenham in 2025–26, with similarly high shares in several other London boroughs. These figures include workers who arrived through different routes and do not measure only recent arrivals.

segments.title: Concerns about retention
segments.body: Care-sector representatives warn that settlement requirements, including a £25,000 earnings threshold for some workers, could make it harder to retain staff. One care provider says about 40 of its 50 employees are migrant workers and that recruiting locally has been difficult. The report says the government has exempted some care workers who arrived before May 2025 from its proposed longer settlement wait, subject to conditions.

content.headline: Police open investigation into fresh allegations against David Walliams
content.shortHeadline: Police investigate fresh allegations against David Walliams
content.standfirst: The Metropolitan Police says it has received allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving the comedian and author. Walliams denies the claims and says he has not engaged in grooming.

image.caption: David Walliams, who denies the allegations reported against him.

sources.originalTitle: David Walliams investigated by police over alleged serious sexual offences

segments.body: The Metropolitan Police says it has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving David Walliams, and that specialist officers are supporting those who have come forward. The force says the allegations are separate from those in reports by ITV News and The Guardian, but detectives are also reviewing that reporting.

Walliams’s lawyers say he never groomed young women and that allegations of serious criminal conduct are false. The reported claims date back to 2003. The police investigation is ongoing; no findings have been made.

content.headline: Three women report rare, life-threatening infections after C-sections
content.shortHeadline: Three women report rare infections after C-sections
content.standfirst: TV 2 reports three cases of severe infections after caesarean births at hospitals in Zealand. The cases raise questions about recognition and treatment, but experts caution that they do not establish a common source or how often this occurs.

sources.originalTitle: Kødædende bakterier rammer kvinder

segments.body: Three women developed life-threatening infections after caesarean births at hospitals in Roskilde and Hvidovre, TV 2 reports. Two cases occurred at Roskilde within about six weeks of each other. The women required emergency treatment; some had organs removed. One woman’s family says she continues to be affected by the experience.

segments.title: What is not yet known
segments.body: A professor interviewed by TV 2 says the cases show that such infections can occur, but cautions against concluding that they are frequent or share a source. He says emergency surgery can involve different conditions from planned procedures, and that rapid recognition and treatment are crucial. The report does not establish a common cause for the cases.

content.headline: Denmark plans targeted leasing subsidy for lower-income rural EV drivers
content.shortHeadline: Denmark plans EV leasing aid for rural, low-income drivers
content.standfirst: A proposed three-year scheme would use 450m kroner to help lower-income people outside major cities lease electric cars. The agreement sets out a plan, with eligibility details still to be negotiated.

sources.originalTitle: Billigere elbiler på vej til udvalgte grupper af danskere

segments.body: A government agreement with Enhedslisten and Alternativet proposes setting aside 450m kroner for a three-year electric-car leasing trial from 2028 to 2030. It is aimed at lower-income drivers outside the largest cities who switch from petrol or diesel cars. The agreement is due to be presented later on Saturday, and detailed rules remain to be worked out.

segments.title: A limited trial
segments.body: The plan currently covers leasing, while the parties are also examining whether purchase subsidies could be included. The government intends to seek additional money from the EU’s social climate fund. The report describes similar targeted support schemes in Sweden and France.

content.headline: Dane alleges ChatGPT legal advice led to eviction in US lawsuit
content.shortHeadline: Dane says ChatGPT advice led to eviction
content.standfirst: A lawsuit filed in California alleges ChatGPT advised a Danish tenant to withhold rent and assured him he could not be evicted. The claims have not been tested in court, and OpenAI has not answered the specific allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Dansk mand siger, at ChatGPT fik ham smidt ud af sin bolig - nu sagsøger han amerikansk gigant

segments.body: A 60-year-old man from southern Zealand alleges in a lawsuit against OpenAI that ChatGPT advised him during a dispute with his landlord, including telling him to stop paying rent. The complaint says the chatbot drafted messages and repeatedly assured him he was protected from eviction. The man was evicted after Danish courts ruled against him, according to the complaint and court documents reviewed by DR.

segments.title: The case is at an early stage
segments.body: The lawsuit alleges the man exchanged more than 41,000 messages with ChatGPT and seeks damages as well as changes to how the chatbot handles legal disputes and delusional beliefs. OpenAI did not respond to DR’s specific questions about the claims; it said it had strengthened ChatGPT’s responses in sensitive and urgent situations. The company has not yet filed its response in court.

content.headline: Shipwreck finds illuminate Danish slave trade and shipboard hierarchy
content.shortHeadline: Wreck finds trace Danish slave trade and hierarchy
content.standfirst: Archaeologists have recovered a shoe sole and trade objects from the wreck of Havmanden, a Danish slave ship lost in 1683. The sole may have belonged to the ship’s governor, but its owner cannot be confirmed.

image.caption: A recovered shoe sole may have belonged to governor Jørgen Iversen Dyppel.

sources.originalTitle: Skosål fra dansk slaveskib vækker opsigt

segments.body: Marine archaeologists working with Swedish colleagues found objects on the wreck of Havmanden in the Swedish archipelago. The ship ran aground after a mutiny in 1683, during which governor Jørgen Iversen Dyppel and other officers were thrown overboard. A shoe sole recovered from the wreck may have belonged to the governor.

segments.title: Evidence of trade and status
segments.body: A shoe specialist says the sole’s quality suggests it belonged to one of only a few people among the roughly 140 on board who could have afforded such footwear. Archaeologists also found two manillas, metal rings used as currency in West African trade, which the National Museum says connect the wreck to European slave-trading and Danish colonial activity.

content.headline: Survey: four in 10 home-care workers say they have been monitored
content.shortHeadline: Survey: four in 10 home-care workers monitored
content.standfirst: A survey of FOA members in social and health care found that four in 10 home-care workers said they had been monitored at work in the past two years. The union is calling for clearer rules and consent.

sources.originalTitle: Ansatte i hjemmeplejen bliver overvåget, viser undersøgelse

segments.body: Four in 10 home-care workers who took part in a new survey of FOA members said they had been monitored at work at least once in the past two years. Respondents described fixed cameras as well as recordings made on phones, watches and other devices. The results are from union members, not a survey of all care workers.

segments.title: Calls for clearer safeguards
segments.body: FOA says relatives were behind the monitoring in seven out of 10 reported cases and argues that filming workers without consent should be restricted. Its sector chair says some staff did not know they were being recorded. The survey does not establish how common each type of monitoring is across the full home-care workforce.

content.headline: Influencers apologise after unapproved KitKat ad filmed on DR set
content.shortHeadline: Influencers apologise over KitKat ad filmed on DR set
content.standfirst: A paid KitKat promotion was filmed during a DR production without the production’s knowledge, according to DR. The influencers’ agent apologised; KitKat says it approved the content expecting that permissions were in place.

image.caption: Josefine Høgh is a presenter on DR programmes.

sources.originalTitle: Josefine Høgh og resten af stor produktion udnyttet af influencer-duo
Josefine Høgh udnyttet af influencere

segments.body: DR says influencers Lucas Georg Christiansen and Nicolai “Frommerjoe” From filmed a paid KitKat promotion on the set of an upcoming programme without the production’s knowledge or consent. The video included host Josefine Høgh and was removed after DR contacted the broadcaster’s press office. The agent says only From was the official sender of the campaign.

segments.title: Questions over permissions
segments.body: The influencers’ agent apologised to Høgh and said the process would be tightened. KitKat’s Nordic brand manager said the company had seen and approved the content on the understanding that permissions were in place, and said the influencer was responsible for obtaining them. A legal professor told DR the use of the set and Høgh without consent could breach marketing rules; that question is for the courts to decide.

content.headline: Danish motorists may not get full benefit of planned fuel-tax cut
content.shortHeadline: Danish fuel-tax cut may not fully reach motorists
content.standfirst: FDM warns that oil companies could retain part of a planned cut to petrol and diesel duty. The tax minister says he will monitor prices, but the reduction is not due to take effect until 2027 under the reported agreement.

sources.originalTitle: Bilister risikerer at blive snydt for billigere brændstof trods ny aftale

segments.body: A planned cut of about two kroner per litre in petrol and diesel duty from 2027 could save some drivers money, but FDM warns that not all of the reduction may reach motorists. It points to a German study in which between 78% and 83% of a similar tax cut was reflected in pump prices.

Tax minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt acknowledges that consumers may not receive the full benefit and says he will watch how prices change. He says he will not rule out involving competition authorities. The report says the cut is planned for one year; a possible earlier start would require parliamentary approval.

content.headline: Man arrested after 21-year-old woman found seriously injured in Aarhus
content.shortHeadline: Man arrested after woman found injured in Aarhus
content.standfirst: A 54-year-old man contacted police and was arrested after a young woman was found badly injured on a road in western Aarhus. Her condition is stable, but she has serious injuries; police are still investigating.

sources.originalTitle: 54-årig anholdt efter påkørsel af ung kvinde fredag aften
Mulig flugtbilist i Aarhus anholdt

segments.body: A 54-year-old man has been arrested after contacting police in connection with the case of a 21-year-old woman found seriously injured on Åby Ringvej in Aarhus on Friday. Police say he came forward after reading about the case in the media and have found a vehicle they believe was involved.

The woman’s condition is now stable and she is expected to survive, although she remains seriously injured. Police are investigating whether other drivers may also have hit her and are seeking witnesses. The arrested man’s custody status had not been decided at the time of the report.

content.headline: Echo & the Bunnymen return with a new album — and old tensions
content.shortHeadline: Echo & the Bunnymen return amid old tensions
content.standfirst: After 12 years, Apples for Isaac brings a burst of psych-pop energy. Ian McCulloch says he wrote and played much of it himself, while his account of guitarist Will Sergeant’s role points to a band relationship still under strain.

image.caption: Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen.

sources.originalTitle: Ian McCulloch: ‘Will Sergeant isn’t the heart of Echo & The Bunnymen. He’s the spleen’

segments.body: Echo & the Bunnymen’s first album in 12 years, Apples for Isaac, arrives with a tune-rich psych-pop sound that Ian McCulloch calls “alive and now”. In an interview, the 67-year-old singer describes writing and producing the record himself and playing most of the instruments, with late Blondie drummer Clem Burke on most tracks.

segments.title: A disputed partnership
segments.body: McCulloch says founding guitarist Will Sergeant plays on four tracks and was largely outside the songwriting process. Sergeant has separately described being ostracised from that process and a long-running undercurrent of animosity. McCulloch insists their current touring relationship is good, but his account leaves the creative partnership looking unsettled.

content.headline: Cristale’s debut mixtape brings every side of her story into focus
content.shortHeadline: Cristale puts her whole story into her debut mixtape
content.standfirst: The Brixton rapper’s route to Clear Intentions ran through football, art and acting, as well as music. She describes a project that moves beyond drill to reflect on family, relationships and the pressures of work.

image.caption: Rapper Cristale.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale

segments.body: Cristale has released her debut mixtape, Clear Intentions, after several attempts to complete a full-length project. The 25-year-old rapper, who grew up in Brixton, moves beyond the drill sound of her early work, drawing on grime, hip-hop, melodic guitar and touches of R&B. She says she left out guest artists because she wanted to tell this part of her story herself.

segments.title: Several paths to music
segments.body: Before committing to music, Cristale played football for Crystal Palace’s academy and studied art and illustration while working long hours. She also acted in Top Boy and The Kitchen. She says her mixtape takes stock of the relationships in her life, and speaks about being judged and underestimated as a young Black woman from Brixton.

content.headline: Sheherazaad turns Urdu folk traditions into shadowy, reverb-soaked music
content.shortHeadline: Sheherazaad gives Urdu folk a shadowy new sound
content.standfirst: On Khudgarzi, the South Asian American singer and composer surrounds spare folk arrangements with a hazy, unsettling production. The review praises her virtuosic voice while noting that some spoken-word passages feel too theatrical.

image.caption: Singer and composer Sheherazaad.

sources.originalTitle: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review – Urdu folk acoustics transformed by an eerie haze of grunge

segments.body: Sheherazaad’s debut album Khudgarzi builds an eerie, introspective sound around Urdu-language singing and sparse acoustic arrangements. Reverb makes tabla, guitar and her keening vocals seem to drift into shadow; the review hears echoes of late-1990s PJ Harvey and Massive Attack’s work with Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, while finding Sheherazaad’s approach distinctive.

Her voice is the album’s strongest thread: a husky lower register anchors “Pakeezah”, while “Andhera” opens into an intricate, full-throated performance. The review is less persuaded by the whispered spoken-word sections, but praises the combination of tabla and South Asian string instruments with cello, guitar, violin and harp.

content.headline: U2’s comeback album finds renewed purpose, but not a new high
content.shortHeadline: U2 find renewed purpose, but not a new peak
content.standfirst: Carnaval De Luz reconnects the band with its familiar anthemic sound after years of creative and reputational trouble. Two reviews hear a more spirited, close-knit group, while differing on how far the record succeeds.

sources.originalTitle: Carnaval De Luz
U2 lost the plot decades ago – their new album finally fixes that

segments.body: U2’s first album of original material in nearly a decade, Carnaval De Luz, turns toward communal, open-hearted songs and the four members’ long history together. Pitchfork hears a lighter, more focused band, with Larry Mullen Jr.’s return after a neck injury helping sharpen the album’s sense of renewed purpose. The i also calls it the group’s best record in 25 years.

segments.title: A qualified return
segments.body: Both reviews find shortcomings. Pitchfork says the record loses momentum in its middle stretch and that the band’s ability to transcend its familiar sound remains out of reach. The i likewise praises the songs but says they lack a unifying hit and questions whether U2 can regain the cultural reach it once had in a fragmented pop landscape.

perspectives.body: The i’s review makes the album’s timing part of its case: it hears a renewed note of hope as U2 confront political events, but argues that the band’s return is solid rather than spectacular, with younger listeners still hard to reach.

content.headline: Judy Collins recalls Joni Mitchell, Leonard Cohen and a life in folk
content.shortHeadline: Judy Collins on Joni Mitchell, Leonard Cohen and folk
content.standfirst: On her farewell tour, the 87-year-old singer remembers recording “Both Sides, Now” before Mitchell, learning from Leonard Cohen and writing through a long career. She sees folk as the storytelling at the heart of pop.

image.caption: Judy Collins.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Joni Mitchell sang Both Sides, Now over the phone to me’: folk music legend Judy Collins on her 87 remarkable years

segments.body: Judy Collins recalls first hearing Joni Mitchell sing “Both Sides, Now” over the telephone in 1967, then recording it the next day. She also describes how Leonard Cohen encouraged her to write her own songs after she recorded “Suzanne”, and remembers a four-month relationship with Stephen Stills that became a lasting friendship.

segments.title: Stories that travel
segments.body: Collins traces her musical outlook to traditional folk, later finding room for songs by the Beatles, Bob Dylan, the Doors and others. “Inside every great pop song, there’s a folk song,” she says. She is still writing, and describes her 2022 album Spellbound — her first collection made up entirely of her own songs — as a particular source of pride.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album gives an actor’s voice room to grow
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson finds her voice in Sound of a Woman
content.standfirst: The actor and musician’s sixth album traces women’s lives through love, grief and ageing. Wilson also reflects on pursuing songwriting later in life, Hollywood’s limited roles for older women and the experience of breast cancer.

image.caption: Rita Wilson.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson’s Sound of a Woman follows a woman’s life from young love through loss and ageing, with songs about friendship, self-doubt and self-acceptance. Wilson says songwriting gave her room to express things that the acting roles offered to her did not, especially as she felt increasingly cast as a mother or supportive friend.

segments.title: Making space for change
segments.body: Wilson says she began pursuing music seriously in her fifties, after feeling creatively stalled in acting. She calls Hollywood ageist and describes the album as an account of becoming the person and artist she wanted to be. One song, “Whose Body Is This?”, reflects on her body after childbirth and breast-cancer treatment.

content.headline: Hiroshi Yoshimura’s Quiet Forest finds wonder in listening closely
content.shortHeadline: Hiroshi Yoshimura finds motion in Quiet Forest
content.standfirst: Inspired by a visit to Washington state’s Hoh Rainforest, this 1996 album moves beyond quiet ambience into playful, softly propulsive synth music. The review hears a revealing portrait of the composer’s curiosity.

sources.originalTitle: Quiet Forest

segments.body: Hiroshi Yoshimura’s Quiet Forest takes its inspiration from the Hoh Rainforest on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, where he was struck by the near-absence of sound beneath the trees. Rather than recreate the landscape literally, the Japanese composer uses synth, vibraphone and gentle percussion to suggest its light, movement and stillness.

segments.title: A more playful side
segments.body: The 1996 record, the last full-length album released during Yoshimura’s lifetime, is more kinetic than his reputation for quiet environmental music might suggest. The review points to its programmed drums and the delicate back-and-forth of flute and synth, hearing an imaginative, playful quality alongside the calm.

content.headline: Grumpy’s Unfindable Ring makes love songs from outsider life
content.shortHeadline: Grumpy turn outsider life into playful love songs
content.standfirst: The Brooklyn group’s genre-hopping album moves between country, folk, electronica and art pop. Pitchfork finds a playful record that makes trans experience part of its everyday world rather than a separate subject.

sources.originalTitle: Unfindable Ring

segments.body: Unfindable Ring shifts from country-inflected songs to electronic textures, indie rock and art pop, with singer Heaven Schmitt changing vocal styles along the way. Pitchfork highlights the opening “OBL”, which begins as a buoyant love song before a trans couple is confronted at a gas station; the encounter makes the song’s devotion feel newly defiant.

segments.title: A world made on its own terms
segments.body: The review describes trans experience not as a single theme but as the air the album breathes: all but one member of the group is trans. Its playful shifts in sound and perspective run through songs about devotion, danger and imagined futures, including “Twenty Five”, which reaches toward a better adulthood for a loved one.

content.headline: Soul Patrol brings a Black Vietnam veterans’ hidden history into view
content.shortHeadline: Soul Patrol reveals the scars of a Black Vietnam unit
content.standfirst: JM Harper’s documentary follows an all-Black long-range reconnaissance team and the lasting trauma of a mission in 1968. Veterans’ memories and archival material bring a little-told experience of war and its aftermath into focus.

image.caption: An archival photograph featured in Soul Patrol.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I relive that mission every single day of my life’: how Black soldiers handled the Vietnam war

segments.body: Soul Patrol follows army team 2/6, company F, 51st Infantry, described in the film as the Vietnam war’s first Black special operations team. The documentary centres on a 1968 reconnaissance mission in the Cu Chi tunnels and the survivors’ enduring guilt over the airstrikes that followed their report. Team member Ed Emanuel says the mission still returns to him every day.

segments.title: A past that does not stay past
segments.body: Director JM Harper combines veterans’ interviews with archival images and footage, using scenes that collapse past and present to convey how memories intrude into ordinary life. The film also considers the discrimination Black soldiers faced in the military and at home, and the lack of support as veterans returned from combat.

content.headline: Elsinore revisits Ian Charleson’s Hamlet as his friends remember the real story
content.shortHeadline: Elsinore and the real story of Ian Charleson’s Hamlet
content.standfirst: Andrew Scott plays the actor who took on Hamlet while dying of Aids; Billie Piper portrays his friend Patsy Pollock. Interviews with people who knew Charleson add details of his illness, the production and the difficult choices behind the performance.

image.caption: Billie Piper, who plays Patsy Pollock in Elsinore.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Women are pitted against each other. It’s a bloodsport’: Billie Piper on industry infighting, Elsinore’s Oscar buzz and thriving on personal crisis
'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids

segments.body: Elsinore dramatises Ian Charleson’s final stage role: Hamlet at London’s National Theatre in 1989, while he was seriously ill with Aids. Andrew Scott plays Charleson, with Billie Piper as his friend, casting director Patsy Pollock. Piper describes Pollock as a close companion who believed in Charleson’s acting talent and helped him through the final months of his life.

segments.title: What the film changes
segments.body: People close to the production add context to the film’s portrayal. Charleson’s doctor Margaret Johnson says she would not have advised him against taking the role, and that the film’s version of her is more senior and forceful than she was. Actor Paul Jesson recalls a supportive company when Charleson disclosed his diagnosis, and says his physical weakness was greater than Scott’s portrayal suggests.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s interviews with Charleson’s doctor and colleagues detail the physical cost of the 24 performances and the supportive response from fellow actors, adding firsthand context to the film’s account.

content.headline: Wicker’s kinky fairy tale makes desire — and gender politics — hard to ignore
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s fairy tale plays desire for laughs and unease
content.standfirst: A woman commissions a husband made of willow in this bawdy fantasy starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård. One review loves its unruly humour but questions its gender politics; the film-makers say domestic labour helped inspire the story.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who pays a basket-maker to create a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård, whose attention and domestic help delight her and unsettle the village. The i’s review relishes the film’s strange, horny comedy while questioning its portrayal of a husband whose desires and agency receive little attention.

segments.title: Fantasy and the work of care
segments.body: The film-makers tell the BBC that the story’s domestic arrangements took on new significance after they became parents, as conversations about household labour and its mental load grew more familiar. A cultural commentator sees Wicker within the broader tradition of romances between women and monstrous or unconventional partners, where desire can unsettle ideas about beauty and power.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s interviews with the film-makers and commentators place the wicker husband in a wider monster-romance tradition and connect the story’s appeal to current debates about care and domestic labour.

content.headline: Heartland gives Jessica Chastain a country-music mystery that loses its way
content.shortHeadline: Jessica Chastain’s Heartland is more miss than hit
content.standfirst: Chastain plays a former country star drawn back to Nashville to search for her missing niece. The review enjoys the film’s occasional sense of place and fierce lead performance, but finds its mystery generic and its final act inert.

image.caption: Jessica Chastain in Heartland.

sources.originalTitle: Heartland review – Jessica Chastain’s Netflix country music thriller is more miss than hit

segments.body: In Heartland, Jessica Chastain plays Misty Jones, a former country singer who returns to Nashville to search for her missing niece. The film reaches for tensions between the city’s musical identity and its image of white, Christian Americana, and uses real venues and musicians to give the setting some texture.

The review finds Chastain compelling as an angry, wounded performer, but says the mystery relies on familiar clues and turns toward a predictable path. Country songs and live-music scenes offer flashes of character; overall, the film struggles to sustain interest and lands closer to background entertainment than a hit.

content.headline: Darth Vader’s screen-used lightsaber sells for a record $4.875m
content.shortHeadline: Darth Vader lightsaber sets a $4.875m auction record
content.standfirst: The prop used in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, including the “I am your father” scene, sold for nearly five times its $1m estimate. The auction house says it is a record for an on-screen Star Wars item.

image.caption: The lightsaber used by Darth Vader in two Star Wars films.

sources.originalTitle: Darth Vader’s lightsaber, used in Star Wars movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, sells for nearly $5m

segments.body: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold for $4.875m at Heritage Auctions’ “Ultimate Star Wars auction”. It appeared in the famous “I am your father” scene and had been estimated to sell for more than $1m.

Heritage Auctions said the sale set a world auction record for an on-screen Star Wars prop, surpassing the $3.75m paid for Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back in July. Twenty-seven lightsaber props were offered at the event.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve looks back at the role that nearly came too late
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the role that changed her career
content.standfirst: Reinsve was considering leaving acting when Joachim Trier offered her the lead in The Worst Person in the World. She recalls a playful shoot that reshaped her career and discusses the very different challenge of playing a mother in Fjord.

image.caption: Renate Reinsve.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve says she thought her appearance at Cannes in 2021 for The Worst Person in the World might be her last red carpet: she was planning to quit acting after struggling to find film work. Director Joachim Trier called with the lead role the day after she made that decision. The film’s success changed her career.

segments.title: A different kind of role
segments.body: Reinsve remembers the Oslo shoot as playful and emotionally open, with scenes that resonated strongly with people on set. In her latest film, Fjord, she plays Lisbet, a quiet evangelical Christian mother whose children are taken amid allegations of abuse. Reinsve says she was drawn to the character’s stillness and to the film’s refusal to dictate what audiences should think.

content.headline: November’s films: from Ian Charleson’s Hamlet to a new Hunger Games prequel
content.shortHeadline: November films: Elsinore, Hunger Games and more
content.standfirst: A month-ahead guide ranges from Andrew Scott’s portrayal of Ian Charleson to a new Hunger Games prequel, with studio releases, festival discoveries and smaller dramas among its picks.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: The month’s film selection includes Elsinore, with Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson during his final Hamlet, and Sunrise on the Reaping, a Hunger Games prequel starring Joseph Zada and Ralph Fiennes. The guide also points to new work from directors including David Fincher, Martin McDonagh and Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

Other recommendations span genres and budgets: Club Kid, a comedy-drama about a New York party promoter who meets the son he never knew; Being Heumann, about disability-rights activist Judith Heumann; and the thriller Josephine, about a child who witnesses a sexual assault. The guide includes release dates across several countries and platforms.

content.headline: Honey turns Killing Eve’s Carolyn Martens into a flirty Cold War spy
content.shortHeadline: Honey gives Killing Eve’s Carolyn a camp spy origin
content.standfirst: The BBC prequel sends a young Carolyn to East Berlin as a honeypot, mixing espionage with pop songs, jokes and knowingly anachronistic dialogue. The review enjoys its camp style while finding its spycraft and history more playful than convincing.

image.caption: Ann Skelly as Martha in Honey.

sources.originalTitle: Honey: this flirty, kinky Killing Eve prequel should have been called Carré on Spying

segments.body: Honey, a prequel to Killing Eve, follows a young Carolyn Martens, renamed Martha Schmitt and sent to East Berlin in 1982. Her assignment is to seduce influential men and photograph them for western intelligence. The Guardian’s review finds the show bright, flirty and stylish, with Ann Skelly as Martha and Rory Kinnear as her handler.

segments.title: Style before spy realism
segments.body: The series treats East Germany as a playful backdrop for dressing up, banter and light kink. Its anachronistic jokes and implausible tradecraft will not satisfy spy purists, the review argues, but the mismatch is part of its camp appeal. The show is broadcast on BBC One on 14 November.

content.headline: The Body mixes Catholic-school politics with a Satanic panic
content.shortHeadline: The Body brings teen drama and occult chaos together
content.standfirst: A Halloween party at a Catholic school turns dangerous in Netflix’s eight-part drama, where social rivalries, queer desire and supernatural scares compete for attention. Its familiar teen-film references are balanced by a sharp feel for adolescent uncertainty.

image.caption: The students of The Body.

sources.originalTitle: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals

segments.body: The Body begins at a Catholic school in 2004, where dance-team leaders Anya and Elise hold social power and outsider Lisbeth longs to join them. A Halloween party at an abandoned convent turns chaotic after an initiation ritual leaves Grace comatose and other students suffering hallucinations and seizures.

segments.title: Adolescence under pressure
segments.body: The review sees the show’s occult panic as an extension of the students’ own social and emotional turmoil, with familiar teen-film touchstones and a vivid early-2000s setting. It praises the central performances and queer coming-of-age tensions, while finding the eight episodes sluggish and some side characters less compelling.

content.headline: This week’s streaming picks include The Altruists and a final Yellowjackets
content.shortHeadline: Streaming picks: The Altruists, Yellowjackets and more
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s weekly guide ranges from a Sam Bankman-Fried drama and the final season of Yellowjackets to stories about Belfast care workers and a drug-overdose helpline.

image.caption: Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Altruists dramatises the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the relationship between Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison. Yellowjackets returns for a fourth and final season, while Rewarding follows two under-resourced Belfast care workers in a quieter comedy-drama.

The guide also recommends The Hotline, a documentary about volunteers who stay on the phone with people using drugs to help prevent overdose, alongside a Christian drama about the life of Jesus and a new season of Percy Jackson. It notes where and when the selected shows are available to stream.

content.headline: Black Doves’ cast explain why viewers root for its murderous spies
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves: the appeal of its murderous antiheroes
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley and the cast discuss the Netflix thriller’s mix of gunplay, humour and emotional fallout. Its second season puts Helen’s marriage and her search for her missing handler alongside another dangerous mission.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Black Doves returns with Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, navigating riskier assignments after her husband becomes prime minister. Helen must find her missing handler while managing growing mistrust at home; Sam, played by Ben Whishaw, takes on a kill list in exchange for freedom from prison.

segments.title: Violence and sympathy
segments.body: Knightley describes the show’s violence as video-game-like until a death is brought into focus. Creator Joe Barton says audiences can accept characters who kill when the stories acknowledge the moral grey area and make those characters compelling. Ambika Mod joins the season as a rogue agent who becomes Helen’s reluctant ally.

content.headline: A guide to foreign-language dramas worth streaming now
content.shortHeadline: Foreign-language dramas to stream from around the world
content.standfirst: This selection ranges from French crime and Spanish dark comedy to a Latvian period drama, Korean family saga and Danish business story. The guide also notes where to find each series and flags when streaming services default to dubbing.

sources.originalTitle: The 11 best foreign-language dramas to stream now

segments.body: The recommendations include Lupin, a glossy French heist series; a Spanish dark comedy about women in crisis; and a Latvian drama set in Soviet-occupied Riga. Other picks include the Danish story of an electric-hair-curler entrepreneur and a German small-town mystery about parents investigating their daughter’s disappearance.

The selection also reaches further afield, with a Korean family saga spanning decades and a crime drama set in Martinique, where dialogue mixes French and local Martinican Creole. The guide notes that Prime Video may default some German-language series to English dubbing, which viewers can change to hear the original dialogue.

content.headline: Patricia Hodge on comedy, career and becoming a mother later in life
content.shortHeadline: Patricia Hodge on Miranda, Thatcher and motherhood
content.standfirst: The actor reflects on roles from The Life and Loves of a She-Devil to Miranda, and on the long wait to have children. At 79, she is celebrating the arrival of a new grandson.

image.caption: Actor Patricia Hodge.

sources.originalTitle: Patricia Hodge on conceiving at 45: ‘It was a test of endurance’

segments.body: Patricia Hodge discusses playing characters as different as Mary Fisher in The Life and Loves of a She-Devil, Margaret Thatcher in The Falklands Play and Penny in Miranda. She credits the sitcom with helping women feel freer to laugh at their own silliness, and remembers the pleasure of making audiences laugh on stage.

segments.title: A long-awaited family
segments.body: Hodge says she struggled to conceive before having her first son at 42 and her second at 45, describing the experience as “a test of endurance”. The interview catches her on the day her second grandson is born, an arrival she describes with delight.

content.headline: Monty Don’s Gardeners’ World farewell marks the end of an era
content.shortHeadline: Monty Don says goodbye to Gardeners’ World
content.standfirst: After 23 years presenting Gardeners’ World, Don’s final episode closes a long run built on calm advice, familiar routines and his Herefordshire garden. The review argues that his personal style made the programme a weekly comfort for viewers.

image.caption: Monty Don in Gardeners’ World.

sources.originalTitle: There will never be another Monty Don

segments.body: Monty Don presents his final Gardeners’ World after 23 years at the programme’s helm. The i’s tribute recalls the familiar opening scenes in his Herefordshire garden, his practical advice and his understated humour, which helped make the gardening show a calming Friday-night ritual.

segments.title: A distinctive presence
segments.body: Don came to gardening without formal training and has spoken openly about depression and other health challenges. The article says his willingness to admit mistakes and his attachment to one garden helped viewers feel invited into the work, rather than made to measure themselves against an ideal.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future: how the long-running show lost momentum
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest pause
content.standfirst: With its Disney+ partnership over, no new Doctor in place and a Christmas special cancelled, the BBC series is off air. Fans and former contributors consider what failed — and what the show might need to return.

image.caption: Actors who have played the Doctor, from Christopher Eccleston to Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has fallen silent since its 2025 series, with the BBC ending its Disney+ partnership and cancelling a planned Christmas special. No new Doctor has been announced, and the corporation is seeking another company to help fund future production. The article describes a series with no clear return date.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: Fans and former contributors point to a combination of factors: confusing scripts, changing showrunners, falling viewing figures and an unsuccessful attempt to scale the show for a global streaming audience. Longtime fan Frank Skinner says the series does not need a huge budget simply to tell a good story, and wants it back on screen without a major overhaul of its origins.

content.headline: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer finds a gentle joy in restoring a small town
content.shortHeadline: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer makes restoration its pleasure
content.standfirst: This gentle game sends a raccoon dog on a BMX to deliver parcels and repair a local shrine. Its slow routines and familiar paths become a calming reward, despite some awkwardly implemented mini-games.

image.caption: A raccoon dog rides through Tanuki: Pon’s Summer.

sources.originalTitle: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time

segments.body: In Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, a raccoon dog takes a post-office job to help pay for repairs to an ancient shrine before a local festival. Most days involve collecting parcels, cycling around a small Japanese town and making sure deliveries reach the right people.

segments.title: Getting to know a place
segments.body: The game’s satisfaction comes less from levelling up than from learning the town’s paths and becoming part of its routines. Fishing and wood-chopping mini-games add variety, though the review finds some controls awkward. The BMX is a particular pleasure, encouraging exploration instead of fast travel.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto became more than a crime game by turning cities into worlds
content.shortHeadline: How Grand Theft Auto grew into a world of its own
content.standfirst: The series has grown from a top-down car-crime game into a densely observed vision of American life. Critics and writers point to its contradictions, cultural references and unhurried freedom as central to its lasting appeal.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto began in 1997 as a Scottish-made game about stealing cars in fictional US cities. Across later entries, its worlds became more detailed and open, from New York-inspired Liberty City to Los Santos, a vision of southern California. The Guardian traces how those settings and the freedom to explore them helped define the series.

segments.title: A city to inhabit
segments.body: The article argues that GTA’s appeal is not only its crime stories or film references, but also the time between missions: driving aimlessly, watching the landscape change or discovering small details. Literary critic Christopher Byrd describes the series as a place players can dwell in, while other contributors connect its crime and rule-breaking to the way cities work.

segments.title: Contradictions on a vast scale
segments.body: GTA satirises consumerism while generating enormous commercial success, and depicts America through the perspective of a studio based in Edinburgh. The article sees those contradictions as part of the series’ artistic force, rather than problems that can simply be resolved.

content.headline: The Ocarina of Time midnight launch brought Zelda fans together — then tested a
content.shortHeadline: Zelda fans queue for Ocarina of Time — and wait
content.standfirst: Hundreds gathered on London’s Oxford Street for early copies and collectibles from the Switch 2 remake. The shared excitement made the launch feel like a return to an older kind of fandom, even as delays left some waiting until 2am.

image.caption: Fans gather for a Zelda game launch.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: Around 500 fans queued outside an Oxford Street Argos for the midnight release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. The writer joined them for a copy, a limited keyring and a replica of the original game box, describing the launch as a rare chance for players to gather around a shared enthusiasm.

segments.title: The wait after midnight
segments.body: The queue moved slowly, and the shop was still out of reach for some after 2am. Staff said people who missed out on the limited box could leave their details to receive one by post. The writer’s initial nostalgia for midnight launches faded into frustration, though he notes that fans at the Paris event were promised no replacement box at all.

content.headline: AI helps researchers uncover hundreds of results in Gödel’s notebooks
content.shortHeadline: AI helps decode Gödel’s notebooks
content.standfirst: A logician using Claude to examine Kurt Gödel’s difficult shorthand says the notebooks contain hundreds of previously unknown mathematical results. The claims are being checked, and their historical significance is not yet settled.

image.caption: Kurt Gödel, whose unpublished notebooks are being examined with AI.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

segments.body: After years of slow work on 1,009 pages of Gödel’s densely written notebooks, Finnish logician Jan von Plato enlisted the AI model Claude. It produced a digest in days, he says, identifying 663 theorems for which Gödel had a proof, a sketch or an idea. Von Plato says the notebooks also point to questions in logic that went unexplored for decades.

segments.title: Checking the claims
segments.body: Von Plato says he checked Claude’s work page by page and tested reconstructed proofs with Coq, software that verifies mathematical proofs. Of the 663 results, he says about 400 were verified as stated, about 200 needed repair and about 50 were false. Logician Joel David Hamkins, who has not seen the reconstruction, said its historical importance—and how much belongs to Claude rather than Gödel—remains for historians to assess.

content.headline: SpaceX Starship launches, but booster splashes down instead of being caught
content.shortHeadline: Starship launches; booster misses planned catch
content.standfirst: Flight 15 began a planned test of Starship’s reusability, but its lower booster was diverted into the Gulf of Mexico. At the time of the report, the upper stage was still expected to attempt a return to Starbase.

image.caption: SpaceX’s Starship Flight 15 lifts off from Starbase in Texas.

sources.originalTitle: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse

segments.body: SpaceX launched its 407-foot Starship from Texas on Friday. The company had planned to catch both the lower booster and upper stage in the launch tower’s mechanical arms. Instead, the booster, Super Heavy, splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The reason for the diversion was not known in the report.

The upper stage was expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over roughly 22 hours before an attempted catch at Starbase. If successful, that would be the first catch of the Starship upper stage; earlier tests had focused on retrieving the booster. The report does not establish whether the planned return succeeded.

content.headline: Hundreds of children in England receive prescriptions for weight-loss drugs
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds of children prescribed weight-loss drugs
content.standfirst: An investigation found prescriptions for GLP-1 medicines among children under 12 as well as older teenagers. The figures are incomplete, and specialists stress that treatment for children needs close supervision and long-term monitoring.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss jabs, figures show

segments.body: NHS data obtained by the Guardian show 419 GLP-1 prescriptions were issued to under-18s in England in the 2025–26 financial year, including 10 for children under 12. From April to July this year, there were 341 prescriptions for children, 15 of them under 12. The figures cover community prescriptions, not private treatment, hospitals or prisons, and do not establish whether every prescription was primarily for weight loss.

segments.title: Specialist care and limited evidence
segments.body: Doctors quoted in the report say these medicines are used for some children with severe obesity and related health problems, often after other support has not helped. They call for specialist care and monitoring of growth, puberty, nutrition, mental health and side effects. Long-term evidence in growing children remains limited; the World Health Organization’s recent guidance says obesity medicines should not be given to children under 10.

content.headline: A broader obesity diagnosis could reduce mistakes made by BMI alone
content.shortHeadline: A broader test could improve obesity diagnoses
content.standfirst: An analysis of health records from more than 800,000 people suggests that combining BMI with waist measurements and checks on organ function may distinguish health risks more accurately than BMI alone.

sources.originalTitle: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’

segments.body: A study using records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain found that BMI alone may miss obesity in 5–9% of adults and wrongly classify as obese up to 3%. The alternative approach combines BMI with measures such as waist size, then distinguishes between excess body fat that is impairing organ function and fat that poses a risk but has not yet caused such problems.

segments.title: A more detailed assessment
segments.body: The researchers followed health records for up to 15 years. They report that 80–90% of people classified as having pre-clinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over the next decade. The approach would take more work from clinicians, and the researchers argue it could help tailor care; the report does not show that every health service has adopted it.

content.headline: US flight halt highlights risks in ageing air-traffic communications
content.shortHeadline: US flight halt highlights ageing systems
content.standfirst: A communications problem affecting several US air-traffic control centres led the FAA to halt departing flights nationwide for nearly five hours. Flights resumed, but the underlying cause was still under investigation.

image.caption: A nationwide FAA ground stop halted departing US flights.

sources.originalTitle: FAA Lifts National Ground Stop for All US Airports, but Many Flights Still Canceled

segments.body: The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide stop to US departures on Friday, citing communication issues affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The stop was lifted after nearly five hours, but thousands of cancellations and delays followed. Officials said it would take time to restore normal operations.

segments.title: The cause remains unclear
segments.body: Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and the report says the investigation was continuing. US officials pointed to ageing air-traffic equipment, including older switches and routers, as a possible problem; that does not establish the cause of this incident. Speculation about a newly expanded AI traffic-management tool was also unconfirmed.

content.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over access to users’ phone photos
content.shortHeadline: Italy fines Meta €805m over photo access
content.standfirst: Italy’s data-protection authority says Facebook did not clearly tell about 20 million Android users that one app permission let it use gallery photos to suggest posts. Meta has not yet commented in the report.

sources.originalTitle: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos

segments.body: Italy’s Data Protection Authority fined Meta €805m over Facebook’s access to photos and videos on Android phones. The regulator says a single app-wide permission did not make clear that Facebook could use gallery content to suggest posts, affecting about 20 million users. It ordered Meta to turn the feature off by default and seek separate consent within 60 days.

The authority cited the number of people affected and said the issue remained ongoing for users who had not updated the app and some who had already consented. The BBC had sought comment from Meta; the report includes no response.

content.headline: A Swedish data centre reuses heat and runs on renewable power
content.shortHeadline: How a Swedish data centre reuses heat
content.standfirst: A facility in Falun uses renewable electricity and sends excess heat into the town’s district-heating system. Its example shows how local planning can shape data-centre impacts, though the model depends on conditions that may not transfer elsewhere.

image.caption: Construction work at EcoDataCenter’s second site in Borlänge, Sweden.

sources.originalTitle: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?

segments.body: EcoDataCenter says its Falun facility gets its electricity from hydropower and wind and sends some of its excess heat into the local district-heating network. The site also uses wood in part of its construction. The company says the facility was planned with the municipality and local suppliers in mind.

segments.title: The limits of the model
segments.body: The report describes advantages in Sweden, including renewable electricity, a cool climate and established district-heating networks. It also cautions that these conditions are not universal: replicating the approach depends on local power and heat infrastructure, regulation and planning. The facility still uses substantial electricity, and the wider question of how much data-centre capacity is needed remains open.

content.headline: Research suggests Chinese AI models used export-restricted Nvidia chips
content.shortHeadline: Research finds signs of restricted Nvidia chips
content.standfirst: An analysis of model weights found signs that leading Chinese AI systems may have been trained on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The findings do not establish where the chips were used or prove that export rules were broken.

sources.originalTitle: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action
Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal

segments.body: Will DePue of Unemployment Labs says he found Blackwell GPU “fingerprints” in open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group. The research suggests the systems may have been trained on chips restricted from export to China. It does not show that they were trained entirely on those GPUs or establish that the hardware was in China.

segments.title: Access and accountability
segments.body: The report notes that Chinese firms can access computing power through data centres abroad, including in Malaysia, and that the evidence does not by itself prove an export-control violation. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said several agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on an export-control list for months, blaming the Commerce Department for delay. Investigations and questions about Nvidia’s checks on customers remain unresolved.

perspectives.body: The report distinguishes evidence that models bear chip fingerprints from proof of where the chips were used or whether export laws were violated.

content.headline: OpenAI’s ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy items with user approval
content.shortHeadline: ChatGPT agents can shop with user approval
content.standfirst: OpenAI is testing a wallet that lets its Dots agents place purchases for eligible US subscribers. Users review each order and approve it with a security check; fully delegated spending is described as a future plan.

sources.originalTitle: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you

segments.body: OpenAI has begun a limited rollout of ChatGPT Wallet to some US Pro subscribers aged 18 and over with eligible US-issued cards. A user can ask a Dots agent to help choose an item; before checkout, the user reviews the purchase and approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint. OpenAI says the wallet uses a payment token rather than sharing card details with the agent or merchant.

segments.title: Retailer access is a constraint
segments.body: OpenAI says it eventually wants users to set limits or other rules so agents can make some purchases without individual approval. That is not the current arrangement. Some retailers block AI agents, and OpenAI says sites and payment systems will need to support legitimate agent purchases for the feature to work more widely.

content.headline: Anthropic’s Duet agent spots work details but can miss their nuance
content.shortHeadline: An AI work agent helps, but misses nuance
content.standfirst: A hands-on test found that Claude Duet could connect information across email, calendars and documents, but sometimes misread deadlines and mixed unrelated conversations. The reviewer also raises questions about giving an agent access to workplace data.

sources.originalTitle: Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful

segments.body: The Verge reviewer connected Duet to work email, a calendar, Google Docs and Slack. The agent spotted a scheduling clash the reviewer had missed and offered to draft a message. It also overreacted to a story deadline that was not firm and produced inaccurate details in a car-pool recap. The hands-on account suggests the tool can find overlooked connections, but does not reliably understand context.

segments.title: Help without handing over judgment
segments.body: The reviewer found Duet useful as a backstop for personal organisation, not as a replacement for it. Giving the agent access to workplace messages also made the breadth of its access more apparent. The review notes that nuance and tone remain weaknesses and that Anthropic says it is still testing the agent’s judgment about when to contact users.

content.headline: Former OpenAI board member argues AI safety needs more than trusted CEOs
content.shortHeadline: AI safety needs more than trusted CEOs
content.standfirst: Helen Toner says safeguards cannot depend on a single leader or voluntary promises. Her argument spans stronger risk checks, time for safety work and focused regulation, while acknowledging uncertainty about both the technology and the best policy response.

sources.originalTitle: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs

segments.body: Helen Toner, who served on OpenAI’s board before voting to remove Sam Altman, says the episode shows the limits of relying on individual leaders to uphold safety commitments. She argues for structures involving more people and perspectives, and says that if AI safety depends on any one person being trustworthy, “we’re pretty screwed.”

segments.title: Standards, not a blanket pause
segments.body: Toner says companies could do more testing, interpretability research and work on controlling systems, but warns that a broad pause could be difficult to define and enforce and might constrain useful work by smaller actors. She favours clearer risk standards and enough time to meet them before training or releasing more capable systems. She describes very advanced AI as plausible enough to prepare for, not as a settled or precisely timed outcome.

content.headline: Thousands protest in Edinburgh against proposed AI data centres
content.shortHeadline: Edinburgh protest targets AI data centres
content.standfirst: Demonstrators raised concerns about the energy, pollution and local disruption associated with large data centres. The Scottish government says new planning guidance is due before year’s end and that large proposals will require environmental assessments.

image.caption: Protesters march along Edinburgh’s Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres

segments.body: Thousands marched in Edinburgh to oppose large-scale AI data centres, including proposals affecting communities in East Lothian, Falkirk and Dumfries and Galloway. A campaigner from Chapelcross cited concerns about construction disruption, operational noise, electricity use and pollution. A proposed site there could have capacity of 1,000 megawatts, according to the report.

segments.title: Planning and public benefit
segments.body: The Scottish government says it will publish planning guidance before the end of the year and is developing a strategy to maximise public benefit. It says new data-centre applications will be referred to ministers and that projects above 50 megawatts must submit an environmental impact assessment. Innovation Minister Alyn Smith argues that Scotland’s planning system should distinguish its proposals from poorly regulated projects elsewhere.

content.headline: Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2 predicts DNA effects in individual cells
content.shortHeadline: AlphaGenome 2 predicts DNA effects by cell type
content.standfirst: Google DeepMind says its new model can estimate how genetic variants affect different cell types and states. The system is available for non-commercial research, but its reported performance gains are company claims rather than proof of improved treatments.

sources.originalTitle: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease

segments.body: AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million cell profiles across 68 tissues, according to Google DeepMind. The company says the model can predict how genetic variants affect particular cell types and states, and identify nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells as its previous model.

segments.title: A research tool, not a treatment
segments.body: The finer-grained predictions could help researchers investigate how genetic changes relate to disease, but the report does not show that the model has led to new treatments. DeepMind says the system is available through an API for non-commercial research, with a limited preview for commercial research. Its more detailed predictions also cost more to produce than those of its predecessor.

content.headline: Pochettino confirmed as Manchester United manager after emotional USA exit
content.shortHeadline: Pochettino confirmed at Man Utd after tearful USA farewell
content.standfirst: Mauricio Pochettino will take charge at Old Trafford on 18 November, replacing Michael Carrick. He says leaving the USA job was one of the most difficult decisions of his career.

image.caption: Mauricio Pochettino became emotional during a USA news conference.

sources.originalTitle: Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd
Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

segments.body: Manchester United have confirmed Pochettino as their new manager, with the Argentine set to begin on 18 November and contracted until June 2029. He became emotional at a news conference as he described leaving the USA national team as a very sad decision, but said the chance to manage United was difficult to turn down.

segments.title: A demanding approach
segments.body: Toby Alderweireld, who played under Pochettino at Tottenham, says the manager puts the team first and expects players to follow his plan. He also points to a gruelling fitness regime and a high-intensity, front-foot style.

perspectives.body: Alderweireld describes Pochettino as a positive “control freak”, saying he closely follows players’ work on and off the pitch.

content.headline: France edge South Africa 21-19 in Nations Championship thriller
content.shortHeadline: France hold off South Africa in 21-19 thriller
content.standfirst: France ended a five-match losing run against the world champions in Paris, holding on after South Africa fought back in a chaotic second half. The result also strengthens France’s position in the northern hemisphere standings.

sources.originalTitle: France hold nerve to edge past South Africa in thriller

segments.body: France beat South Africa 21-19 at Stade de France, ending their five-match losing run against the world champions. Antoine Dupont’s side scored three tries in an electric first half, with Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Theo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey crossing.

segments.title: A tense finish
segments.body: South Africa rallied after Jasper Wiese was shown a 20-minute red card, with replacement Cobus Reinach and Malcolm Marx scoring tries. Manie Libbok missed the conversion that would have levelled the match, and France held on under late pressure.

The victory dents South Africa’s hopes of reaching the Nations Championship final and leaves France six points clear at the top of the northern hemisphere standings. Les Bleus face Argentina next Saturday.

content.headline: McGinn double gives Scotland 2-1 win over North Macedonia
content.shortHeadline: McGinn scores twice as Scotland beat North Macedonia
content.standfirst: Scotland earned a first home win under Sebastien Pocognoli, but a narrow victory over the group’s bottom side did little to quiet doubts about the team’s progress. Andy Robertson also drew level with Kenny Dalglish’s cap record.

sources.originalTitle: Tough watch as Scotland again battle against their own limitations
Scotland Men's Football Team

segments.body: John McGinn scored twice as Scotland beat North Macedonia 2-1 at Hampden, giving manager Sebastien Pocognoli his first home win. The hosts led after McGinn’s second-half opener, but Elmin Rastoder equalised before McGinn converted a late penalty won by Ben Gannon-Doak.

segments.title: A win with work still to do
segments.body: The result leaves Scotland one point behind Slovenia with one group game remaining. Scotland must travel to Switzerland, while Slovenia visit North Macedonia. Robertson won his 102nd cap, drawing level with Dalglish’s Scotland record.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s match analysis described the performance as a difficult watch, arguing that Scotland’s effort outweighed its precision and that the team still looks uncertain in its system.
